senses: Of a person: overly assertive, bold, or domineering; pushy; also, ostentatious.
Of a thing: noticeable or prominent, especially in a displeasing way.
ety: From Latin obtrūsus + English -ive (suffix meaning ‘of the nature of’, forming adjectives). Obtrūsus is the perfect passive participle of obtrūdō, a variant of obstrūdō (“to push, shove, or thrust against or into”), from ob- (prefix meaning ‘against; towards’) + trūdō (“to push, shove, or thrust”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to push; to thrust”)).
examples: The office manager is an unpleasantly obtrusive individual.
But there was a third principal in this primitive drama, the wife of Essenden, a woman of great energy, great possessiveness and obtrusive helpfulness.

senses: To take oneself to; go or move; repair; resort; have recourse.
ety: From Middle English bitaken, equivalent to be- + take. Cognate with Danish betage (“to take, deprive, cut off”), Swedish beta (“to take, deprive, cut off”).
examples: I was glad of my arrival for I was wearied with the way, and yellow of face for weakness and want; but my plight was pitiable and I knew not whither to betake me.

senses: A staff topped with a conical ornament, carried by Bacchus or his followers.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos). Doublet of thyrse, torse, and torso.
examples: As good to grow on graves / As twist about a thyrsus.
The champagne was done, and she upturned the bottle to hold it like a thyrsus.

senses: A mouth or aperture, such as of a tube, pipe, etc.; an opening.
One of the natural external openings of the human or animal body.
ety: From Middle French, from Old French, from Late Latin ōrificium (“an opening, literally the making of a mouth”), compound of ōs (“mouth”) + faciō (“to make”).
examples: The plug in the orifice of the tube was temporarily removed and the mirror carefully cleaned.
The maw-worm could emerge unexpectedly from any orifice, including, most alarmingly, the corner of people's eyes.

senses: A subarctic zone of evergreen coniferous forests situated south of the tundras and north of the steppes in the Northern Hemisphere.
ety: From Russian тайга́ (tajgá), from South Siberian Turkic (Altai region, for example the Altay or Shor language, cf Khakas: тағ (tağ)), or alternatively Yakut тайга (tayga, “untraversable forest”). Doublet of Tayga.
examples: The mountains run from the Arctic Island of Novaya Zemlya southwards, dividing the endless wastes of the Siberian taiga and the steppes from the Russian platform in the west.
Like the taiga, he was everywhere, and mysterious—a heroic being with unearthly gifts.

senses: Space to stretch the legs while seated.
Freedom to move or grow.
ety: From leg + room.
examples: The lack of legroom on international flights can be a health hazard as blood clots can form from not being able to move around.
Highlighted benefits include high quality seating, more legroom, more luggage space and a fixed buffet with kitchen providing a range of catering.
These guidelines provided some more legroom to the pro-religious groups without seriously offending liberals' concerns.

senses: A change in nature, form, or quality.
The spread of something harmful to another location, such as the metastasis of a cancer.
A sudden or rapid transition from one point, topic or argument to another, often to evade an uncomfortable subject or to redirect the discussion.
ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin metastasis (“(rhetoric) rapid or sudden transition from one argument, point, or topic to another”), and from its etymons Koine Greek μετάστασις (metástasis, “(rhetoric) rapid or sudden transition from one argument, point, or topic to another”) and Ancient Greek μετάστασις (metástasis, “change; removal; (medicine) movement of disease, pain, etc., from one part of the body to another”), from μετᾰ- (metă-, prefix denoting change in condition or position) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meth₂) + στᾰ́σῐς (stắsĭs, “condition, state; position”) (ultima
examples: Stayed in her own house, searched her body each morning and examined her conscience each night for progressive symptoms of the metastasis she feared was in her.

senses: To adorn with a mitre.
To unite at an angle of 45°.
ety: From Middle English mytre, from Old French mitre, from Ancient Greek μίτρα (mítra, “headband, turban”). Its use in reference to a counterfeit coin derived from the bishop's mitre stamped upon it. Doublet of Mithras, Mithra, Mitra, and Mehr.
examples: The bartizans have each a peculiar angle shaft on the outer face, which mitres into the string-course at bottom, and probably supported a shield with coat of arms or a crest or other ornament rising above the parapet

senses: Anarchic; chaotic or free-spirited.
ety: From anarchist + -ic.
examples: With the exception of the leader's boppish title tune, the album is filled with anarchistic jazz reduxes of Nichols, Ellington, Kurt Weill, and Cole Porter.

senses: Beyond or on the other side of an ocean.
Crossing an ocean.
ety: From trans- + oceanic.
examples: Guam is a transoceanic territory of the United States.
We took a transoceanic flight.

senses: A problem set forth in the Ancient Greek scholarly tradition.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma). Doublet of problem.
examples: For quotations using this term, see Citations:problemata.

senses: Characterized by percussion; caused by or related to the action of striking or pounding something.
ety: From percuss + -ive.
examples: He massaged her shoulders with a gentle percussive action.

senses: Shabby, squalid, uncared-for.
ety: From English dialectal (Kentish) dingy (“dirty”), of unknown origin, though probably from Middle English *dingy, dungy, from Old English *dyncgiġ (“covered with dung, dirty”), an umlaut form of duncge, dung (“dung”), equivalent to dung + -y, hence a doublet of dungy.
examples: She's looking from Tarquin to Fenella with shining eyes, and I look at the picture interestedly over her shoulder. But to be honest, I can't say I'm impressed. For a start it's really dingy – all sludgy greens and brown

senses: A woman who flirts or plays with people's affections.
ety: Borrowed from French coquette.
examples: She was a big, sexy brunette—as Garcia said, «Something straight out of Degas,» and generally like a beautiful Parisian coquette.
I was playing with him, leading him on, sending him messages of encouragement then turning away from him. I was a tease, a coquette.

senses: Seafire, phosphorescence on the ocean, especially around the Shetland Islands.
ety: From an unattested Norn term *mareld, from Old Norse mǫrueldr, from marr (“sea”) + eldr (“fire”). Compare Icelandic maurildi, Swedish mareld.
examples: This is especially the case in late summer when the sea is aflame with mareel and the boats come and go with illumined wakes while the ghostly fire drips from the oar-blades.

senses: Green in colour.
Abundant in verdure; lush with vegetation.
Inexperienced.
ety: From Middle French verdoyant, from Old French verb verdier, verdoier, from vert (“green”), from Vulgar Latin *virdis, from Latin viridis.
examples: It was a verdant and delightful valley, watered by a rivulet ...
A serene sky and verdant fields filled me with ecstasy.

senses: A supply of food.
The department of an army that supplies provisions for the troops.
A department of the government of the Soviet Union in the early period of its existence.
A territorial and governmental unit of Colombia at some points in its history.
ety: Borrowed from French commissariat.
examples: We gave such dinner-parties as our commissariat allowed; the menu was simplicity itself - " blanket " for every course, cunningly disguised as soup, entree, and, I was going to say, joint.

senses: Playing at courtship; coquetry.
An instance of flirting.
A period of experimentation with or interest in a particular idea or activity.
ety: From flirt + -ation.
examples: The elimination of vacuum-braked wagons would be slowed down, and the Western Region's flirtation with diesel-hydraulic locomotives was questioned.

senses: The minimum number of ten (male) adult Jews required for a communal religious service.
A Jewish prayer service.
ety: From Hebrew מִנְיָן (minyán, “number, count, quorum”).
examples: So without my visit, if Simon didn't attend, a minyan would be hard to come by.
As mourners cannot attend synagogue during shiva, a minyan gathers for morning, afternoon, and evening services in their home.
New people assume leadership positions as required and stay around for as long as the minyan meets their needs.

senses: A crystal of zircon, sometimes used as a false gemstone.
ety: From German Zirkon, possibly via French zircon, formed in the 1780s from Arabic زَرْقُون (zarqūn), borrowed from Middle Persian zlgwn' (/⁠zargōn⁠/). Doublet of jargoon.
examples: A zircon princess, seemed to lost her senses

senses: Disparaging, belittling or derogatory.
ety: From Late Latin peiōrātus (“worsened”, past participle of peiōrāre (“worsen”), from Latin peior (“worse”)) + -ive. Compare French péjoratif (“depreciative, disparaging”). By surface analysis, pejorate + -ive.
examples: These days, on platforms like X, slopulism is a pejorative label often applied to posts by politicians and pundits alike, anyone who shares out lowest-common-denominator ideas designed to appeal to loyal political bases.

senses: A harmonic mode in ancient Greek music, characterized by a particular set of chords and rhythmic patterns.
The soul regarded as a harmonious blend of the parts of the physical body.
ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ᾰ̔ρμονῐ́ᾱ (hărmonĭ́ā). Doublet of harmony.
examples: In 1935, Hamilton trained a chamber orchestra in Stuttgart to perform in the harmoniai.
Socrates argued against the idea of the soul being a harmonia.

senses: To remove a blockage from; to release from being jammed.
ety: From un- + jam.
examples: The printer is still on, which is good because you may need to access features, unjam the printer, or do things that you otherwise cannot do while the thing is printing.

senses: A band passed under the belly of an animal, which holds a saddle or a harness saddle in place.
The part of an animal around which the girth fits.
One's waistline circumference, most often a large one.
A small horizontal brace or girder.
The distance measured around an object; the circumference.
ety: From Middle English girth, gerth, gyrth, from Old Norse gjǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *gerdō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰerdʰ- (“to encircle, enclose; belt”). Cognate with Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌳𐌰 (gairda), Icelandic gjörð. Also related to German Gurt, English gird, Albanian ngërthej (“to tie, bind, fasten”).
examples: He's a lusty, jolly fellow, that lives well, at least three yards in the girth.

senses: A strip of fabric which has been fluted or pleated.
A small ruff of fluted or pleated fabric worn at neck or wrist.
A pile of arched tiles, used to catch and retain oyster spawn.
ety: Borrowed from French ruche, from Middle French rusche, from Old French rusche, from Early Medieval Latin rusca (“bark”), borrowed from Gaulish rūsca, from Proto-Celtic *rūskos (“bark”), from *rukskos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rewk- (“to dig up”), from *Hrew- (“to tear out, dig out”).
examples: Mrs. Newsome wore at operatic hours a black silk dress—very handsome, he knew it was "handsome"—and an ornament that his memory was able further to identify as a ruche.

senses: A divinity, especially a local or presiding god.
An influence or phenomenon at once mystical and transcendent.
ety: Borrowed from Latin nūmen.
examples: It was the solid and immovable tabernacle of the living numen whose son he had known, though but briefly and not intimately, in the flesh, and whose message he accepted with all his heart.

senses: A large flightless parrot, Strigops habroptilus, with greenish plumage, that is nocturnal and native to New Zealand.
ety: Borrowed from Māori kākāpō.
examples: Analyses of the DNA fragments preserved in the moa and kakapo coprolites showed that moa and kakapo fed on fungi.

senses: A flavored, creamy sugar preparation, used for icing cakes or as a base for candies.
A candy or cake filled with such a preparation.
A sugar dough, usually prepared as large sheets (rolled fondant), used in place of icing to cover large areas of cakes, composed of sugar, water, gelatin, glycerine.
The base or flux, in enamel, which is colored throughout by metallic oxide while in a state of fusion.
ety: 19th century. Unadapted borrowing from French fondant (“melting”), from fondre (“to melt”), from Latin fundere (“to melt”).
examples: At Chapter One, these chocolate fondants are served restaurant-style with a crème brulée ravioli and an unusual basil ice cream as well as the warm sauce given.
Stan made a heroic attempt at a tiered cinnamon cake with a rolled fondant icing that came out gray and tore when he draped it over the cake.

senses: A small horse-drawn carriage for hire; a hackney carriage.
ety: Borrowed from French fiacre. From Hôtel de Saint Fiacre, a tavern in Paris operating a horse-carriage service from the 1640s, itself named after the Irish Saint Fiacre (c. 600–670 CE), perhaps from Irish fiach (“raven”).
examples: On the road to Choissi, a fiacre, or hackney-coach, stopped, and out came five or six men, armed with musquets, who took post, each behind a separate tree.
Poor Jim, with his arms folded and his little legs out in the open fiacre, drank in the sparkling Paris noon and carried his eyes from one side of their vista to the other.
The boy who might have fetched us a fiacre was now doing something else, so we had to go back to the station, and there we found only one, which was falling to pieces.

senses: To convert (waste materials, etc.) into new materials or products of higher quality and greater functionality.
To promote into a more productive or useful role.
ety: Blend of up- + recycle or possibly upgrade + recycle.
examples: Recycling in many cases means "downcycling" – in particular cases, however, it can also mean "upcycling".

senses: A black person.
ety: From Cuffee, a personal name formerly common among black Americans.
examples: The war had turned very bitter, and the days of young blacks, or cuffees as they were known, joining up just to escape the ghetto were over.

senses: A henna plant (Lawsonia inermis).
The preparation of this plant used for dyeing.
A temporary skin decoration made with henna.
The practice of applying such decoration, typically as part of a bride or groom's preparations for a wedding.
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani मेहंदी (mehandī) / مہندی (mihandī), from Sanskrit मेन्धिका (mendhikā). First attested in the 19th century.
examples: She was thirteen, a young bride whose small palms had been stained burgundy with mehndi for a man she knew nothing about, not even his name.
Then came the Mehndi ceremony – where henna is painted on the bride's hands and feet, and the bride and groom's family try to outdo each other in singing and dancing.

senses: To spring forward on the hind legs.
To strut about in a showy manner.
ety: From Middle English prancen, prauncen (“to prance”, literally “to show off”), variant of Middle English pranken (“to prank”), thus probably from the same ultimate root as prank. Cognate with Bavarian prangezen, prangssen (“to put on airs”), Alemannic German pranzen (“to strut”).
examples: John's daughter was prancing about the sitting room, practicing for her school dance.

senses: Masturbation.
Ejaculating outside the vagina during intercourse; (the performing of) coitus interruptus.
ety: From Onan + -ism. In the Book of Genesis, Onan, son of Judah, in fulfillment of the laws of levirate marriage was to impregnate his brother Er's widow, Tamar, in order to raise offspring from the union in his brother's name. In order to avoid raising descendants for his late brother, however, Onan "spilled his semen on the ground when he went in to his brother's wife, so that he would not give offspring to his brother" (Genesis 38:9).
examples: This photograph was far superior. A nude woman was sitting on the edge of a desk next to a globe of the world. The suggested onanism with the piece of chalk intrigued Ignatius.

senses: A person, creature or thing that growls.
A small iceberg or ice floe which is barely visible over the surface of the water.
A kind of jug, often with a handle, used to carry beer and preserve carbonation.
A device for checking electrical equipment for short circuits etc.
ety: From growl + -er. Sense "jug" is 19th century American slang, of uncertain origin.
examples: A great ‘growler’ iceberg was sighted this afternoon at a distance of approximately half a mile; the size of a large London house, more or less.
As the cruise ship Explorer was picking its way through the Antarctic sea ice, it hit what experts believe was a "growler" - a huge iceberg shorn from the Antarctic ice shelf.
Includes voltmeters, ammeters, circuit testers, armature tester (external growler), field tester, (internal growler), coil and condenser tester, etc.

senses: A flat-topped seamount.
ety: Coined by Harry Hammond Hess circa 1965 due to their similar appearance to Guyot Hall, the flat-topped geology building at Princeton University, which was in turn named after Swiss-American geologist Arnold Henry Guyot.
examples: It was scored everywhere with canyons, trenches and crevasses and dotted with volcanic seamounts that he called guyots after an earlier Princeton geologist named Arnold Guyot.

senses: Using the senses rather than instruments.
ety: From French organoleptique, from organo- + Ancient Greek ληπτικός (lēptikós, “disposed to take”), from λαμβάνω (lambánō, “to take”).
examples: Organoleptic testing of the cosmetics revealed the presence of lumps in the hand cream.

senses: The act of edifying, or the state of being edified or improved; a building process, especially morally, emotionally, or spiritually.
ety: From Old French, from Latin aedificationem (“building, construction”), an accusative form of aedificatio, from aedificare.
examples: Let euery one of vs please his neighbour for his good to edification.
Caterina Pachetti had been a very pretty women, which she remembered more to her own edification than to that of her friends.

It seems clear that he took great delight in his commonly perceived role as “the No 1 celebrity scientist”; huge audiences would attend his public lectures, perhaps not always just for scientific edification.

senses: A dog of a particular breed originating in Germany.
ety: Borrowed from German Schnauzer.
examples: The five-year-old Giant Schnauzer was also awarded Best in Show at the AKC National Championship in December.

senses: Formulated or enacted by rabbis.
ety: From rabbi + -n- + -ic.
examples: Even though some modern Jews are less interested in rabbinic enactments than the traditions that have explicit roots in Biblical law, most still practice customs that would not exist without rabbinic innovation.

The book significantly extends on Rosenstein’s monumental 1990 work, “The Unbroken Chain,” which focused on the genealogies of the major Ashkenazi rabbinic dynasties from medieval times to the present.
